PAGE 1: Overview

OVERVIEW
========

A Muslim family is wider than mother, father and children. Grandparents, brothers, sisters, uncles, aunts and cousins are also family. In this sub-strand you will name those members, learn a child's duties towards them, and see why keeping the family bond is an act of ibadah.

## Strand 6.0: Muamalaat (Social Relations)
Sub-strand 6.3: Children’s Obligations to Other Family Members
Suggested lessons: 3

## Learning outcomes
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) outline obligations of children to other family members as an act of ibadah
b) assess the significance of fulfilling obligations to other family members
c) appreciate maintaining bond with other family members

## Key inquiry questions
1. Who are the other family members?
2. How do you develop good relationship with other family members?
3. What is the significance of strengthening your relationship with other family members?

## Core competencies
• Communication and collaboration: the skill of listening, speaking and writing enhanced as learners discuss children’s obligations to other family members (e.g. respect, visiting, attending ceremonies, helping and caring for them), in pairs/groups, and write the points in their notebook
• Critical thinking and problem solving: the skill of evaluation and decision making is enhanced as learners discuss the significance of fulfilling obligations to other family members, in pairs/groups.
• Creativity and imagination: the skill of networking enhanced as learners dramatise their obligations to other family members.
• Learn to learn: the skill of sharing learnt knowledge enhanced as learners prepare chart with names of extended family members and hang strategically.

## Values
• Respect: acceptance enhanced as learners respect each other’s opinions while discussing, in groups.
• Responsibility: accountability as learners prepare chart with names of extended family members and hang strategically.

## Pertinent and contemporary issues
• Social cohesion as learners relate well with family and other members of the society.

## Links to other learning areas
• Social Studies as learners fulfil their duties towards family and other members of the society.

## Source
• KICD Grade 4 Islamic Religious Education Curriculum Design (Revised 2024) — Strand 6.0 Muamalaat (Social Relations), Sub-strand 6.3 Children’s Obligations to Other Family Members
• Sahih al-Bukhari: whoever would like his provision increased and his life extended should uphold the ties of kinship

PAGE 2: Lesson 1: Other family members and our duties to them

LESSON 1: OTHER FAMILY MEMBERS AND OUR DUTIES TO THEM
=====================================================

## What you will learn
• Name members of the extended family.
• Outline a child's obligations to those family members.

Curriculum outcomes: a) outline obligations of children to other family members as an act of ibadah

## Introduction
When relatives gather for a wedding, aqiqah or a visit, you meet people who share your grandparents even if they do not live in your house. Islam calls you to know them and to treat them well.

## Notes
### Who the other family members are
Besides parents, a child's family includes:

- Brothers and sisters
- Grandfathers and grandmothers
- Uncles and aunts, on both the father's side and the mother's side
- Cousins
- Other close relatives the family keeps in touch with

These relatives are often called the extended family. In many homes a grandparent or an uncle also helps to raise the children. They are still part of this duty.

### Obligations of children
The learning in this sub-strand names practical duties. They are acts of ibadah when done to please Allah:

- Respect: greet elders first, use polite titles, and do not laugh at their age or their way of speaking.
- Visiting: go with your parents to see relatives, especially the sick and the elderly. Do not wait only for parties.
- Attending ceremonies: join family events such as a wedding, aqiqah or a funeral gathering in the way your parents guide you. Be helpful and well behaved there.
- Helping: carry a chair, serve a drink, look after smaller cousins, or assist a grandparent with a simple task.
- Caring: ask how they are, make dua for the sick, and share what you have when you visit.

### A chart of names
Knowing names is part of the bond. A child who can say "This is my maternal aunt" and "These are my cousins" is ready to keep the tie. Write the names your parents allow you to record. Do not invent relatives, and do not share private family matters in class.

## Key words
• extended family — relatives beyond parents and children, such as grandparents, uncles, aunts and cousins
• maternal — related through the mother
• paternal — related through the father
• ibadah — worship; a good deed done to please Allah

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Sort these people into 'parents' and 'other family members': mother, cousin, father, grandmother, uncle, sister.

Working:
1. Parents are mother and father.
2. The others are family members this sub-strand is about. A sister is part of the household and is also among the relatives a child must respect and help.

Answer: Parents: mother, father. Other family members: cousin, grandmother, uncle, sister.

## Activity: Extended family chart
You will need: Manila paper, Marker pens, Tape to hang the chart
1. In groups, draw a simple chart with spaces for grandparents, parents, uncles, aunts, brothers, sisters and cousins.
2. Each learner adds the names of extended family members that he or she may share in class.
3. Under the chart, write the obligations: respect, visiting, attending ceremonies, helping and caring.
4. Hang the chart where the class can see it, and one learner explains it.

## Practice
1. Name four members of the extended family.
2. State the five kinds of obligation named for children towards other family members.
3. What is the difference between a maternal aunt and a paternal aunt?
4. How can helping at a family ceremony be an act of ibadah?

## Summary
• Other family members include siblings, grandparents, uncles, aunts and cousins.
• Children respect them, visit them, attend family ceremonies, and help and care for them.
• These duties are ibadah when done to please Allah.

### Answers to practice
1. Any four: grandfather, grandmother, uncle, aunt, cousin, and other close relatives. Brothers and sisters may also be named.
2. Respect, visiting, attending ceremonies, helping and caring for them.
3. A maternal aunt is a sister of one's mother. A paternal aunt is a sister of one's father.
4. When it is done to please Allah and to keep good family ties.

PAGE 3: Lesson 2: Why the family bond matters

LESSON 2: WHY THE FAMILY BOND MATTERS
=====================================

## What you will learn
• Explain the significance of fulfilling obligations to other family members.
• State how a Muslim keeps the bond even when relatives live far away.

Curriculum outcomes: b) assess the significance of fulfilling obligations to other family members; c) appreciate maintaining bond with other family members

## Introduction
A rope is strong when every strand is held. Family ties are like that. Islam does not want the strands to be cut.

## Notes
### Keeping ties of kinship
The Prophet (S.A.W) said that whoever would like his provision to be increased and his life to be extended should uphold the ties of kinship (Bukhari). Keeping the bond is called silat al-rahim. Cutting it, without a right cause, is a serious wrong.

Allah commands believers to be careful about family ties. A Muslim does good to relatives because Allah ordered it, not only because they gave a gift last year.

### Why these obligations matter
- They please Allah and are rewarded as ibadah.
- Relatives support one another in sickness, poverty, celebrations and grief.
- Children learn manners, history and faith from grandparents and older relatives.
- Visits and ceremonies stop the family from becoming strangers.
- Respect for elders spreads peace in the home and in the wider community. This is social cohesion: people relate well instead of quarrelling.
- A child who keeps family ties is practising for good citizenship, because the same respect is later shown to neighbours and the community.

### When relatives are far
Distance does not cancel the duty. A family can send salaam through a parent, make dua, share news, and visit when travel is possible. If a relative is unkind, the Prophet's teaching is still to keep the tie in a good way and not to reply to harm with worse harm. Children follow their parents' guidance on visits and do not go to relatives' homes alone without permission.

Appreciating the bond means you are glad to belong to these people, you speak well of them, and you do not gossip about family matters.

## Key words
• silat al-rahim — keeping the ties of kinship with relatives
• kinship — the relationship among members of a family
• social cohesion — people living together in peace and good relationship

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Hawa's grandmother lives in another town. Hawa says, "I cannot visit every week, so I have no duty." What is wrong with this idea, and what can she do?

Working:
1. Distance reduces visits; it does not end silat al-rahim.
2. She can send salaam, make dua, and visit when the family travels.

Answer: The duty remains. She should keep the bond through salaam, dua and visits when they are possible.

## Activity: Why we keep the bond
You will need: Exercise book
1. In pairs, brainstorm the significance of fulfilling obligations to other family members.
2. Write at least four points, including one benefit to the child and one benefit to the whole family.
3. Discuss one way to keep the bond when a relative lives far away.
4. Present your points and listen to the other pairs without interrupting.

## Practice
1. What is silat al-rahim?
2. Give three reasons why fulfilling duties to other family members is important.
3. What did the Prophet (S.A.W) connect with upholding ties of kinship?
4. Name two ways to keep a family bond when relatives live far away.

## Summary
• Silat al-rahim means keeping ties with relatives, and it pleases Allah.
• The bond brings help, learning and peace.
• Distance does not cancel the duty.

### Answers to practice
1. Keeping the ties of kinship with relatives.
2. Any three: it pleases Allah; relatives support one another; children learn from elders; the family does not become strangers; it spreads peace.
3. He said that whoever would like his provision to be increased and his life extended should uphold the ties of kinship.
4. Any two: send salaam, make dua, share news through parents, visit when travel is possible.

PAGE 4: Lesson 3: Practising good relationship with the family

LESSON 3: PRACTISING GOOD RELATIONSHIP WITH THE FAMILY
======================================================

## What you will learn
• Demonstrate obligations to other family members in short scenes.
• Choose ways to maintain the family bond.

Curriculum outcomes: a) outline obligations of children to other family members as an act of ibadah; c) appreciate maintaining bond with other family members

## Introduction
A visit can strengthen a family or embarrass it. The difference is in the greeting, the help you offer, and the way you speak.

## Notes
### How to behave with relatives
- Greet the oldest person first, with Assalamu alaikum, and shake hands or respond in the way your family teaches.
- Sit where you are asked to sit. Do not push cousins aside for the best place.
- Offer help before you are begged: pass plates, fetch water, or keep younger children from the cooking area if an adult asks.
- Listen when an elder is speaking. Do not correct an elder rudely, and do not whisper and laugh about them.
- At a ceremony, follow the programme. Do not wander off, demand money, or use a phone to record people without permission.
- If a grandparent is ill, a short quiet visit, a dua and a small service are better than a noisy crowd.
- Thank the hosts before you leave.

### Building the habit
Choose one relative to remember this month. It may be a grandparent or an aunt. Ask your parent the best way to show care: a visit, a drawn card with salaam, or help on a family day. Do that one thing. Then keep it up.

Good relationship is not only receiving gifts on Eid. It is also being present, useful and polite. When children do this, adults are encouraged to keep the same bond, and the family stays joined. That is the appreciation this sub-strand asks for: valuing the relatives Allah has given you and maintaining the tie.

## Key words
• aqiqah — the celebration and sacrifice for a newborn, held in the way the family observes
• host — the person whose home or event you are visiting
• elder — an older relative who should be greeted and listened to with respect

## Worked examples

### Example 1
At an uncle's house, two cousins start a loud argument over a chair while adults are talking. What should a dutiful child do?

Working:
1. The noise disrespects the elders and the host.
2. A dutiful child stops the fight, offers to share or take another seat, and apologises if needed.

Answer: Quiet the argument, give way on the chair, and show respect to the adults in the room.

## Activity: Drama: a family visit
You will need: A few chairs set out as a relative's sitting room
1. In groups, prepare a short play of a visit to a grandparent or an uncle.
2. Include a greeting, an offer of help, polite listening, and a goodbye.
3. Present the play. The class points out the obligations that were shown.
4. Each learner writes one action he or she will take this month to maintain a family bond.

## Practice
1. Whom should you greet first when you enter a room of relatives?
2. Give three good manners during a family visit or ceremony.
3. Why is a family bond not only about receiving gifts?

## Summary
• Greet elders, help hosts, and listen during visits and ceremonies.
• One real act of care is better than many unused promises.
• Maintaining the bond is how a child appreciates the family Allah has given.

### Answers to practice
1. The oldest person, or the elders, with Assalamu alaikum.
2. Any three: greet elders, sit where you are asked, offer help, listen, do not record people without permission, thank the host.
3. It is also about being present, useful and polite, and about keeping the tie to please Allah.
pages.quiz:
REVISION QUIZ — 6.3 CHILDREN’S OBLIGATIONS TO OTHER FAMILY MEMBERS
========================================

Answer all the questions, then mark yourself on the Answers tab.

1. Which of these is an extended family member?
   A. A classmate
   B. A maternal uncle
   C. A shopkeeper
   D. A bus driver

2. A paternal aunt is…
   A. the sister of one's father
   B. a neighbour
   C. a teacher's wife
   D. a cousin's friend

3. Which set matches the obligations in this sub-strand?
   A. Ignore, gossip, stay away
   B. Respect, visit, help and care
   C. Borrow and never return
   D. Only attend parties

4. When can helping at a family aqiqah be ibadah?
   A. it is done to please Allah
   B. it is done to show off
   C. it is done while insulting cousins
   D. it replaces swalah

5. Silat al-rahim means…
   A. cutting off relatives
   B. keeping the ties of kinship
   C. travelling without permission
   D. hiding from grandparents

6. Give one benefit of fulfilling obligations to other family members.

7. The Prophet (S.A.W) linked upholding kinship ties to which of these?
   A. losing one's family
   B. provision being increased and life being extended
   C. stopping all visits
   D. avoiding elders

8. A grandmother lives far away. How does a child maintain the bond?
   A. forgetting her
   B. sending salaam, making dua and visiting when the family can
   C. speaking badly about her
   D. refusing to learn her name

9. At a relative's house the dutiful child…
   A. pushes to get the best chair
   B. greets the elders and offers help
   C. records everyone without asking
   D. argues with adults

10. Appreciating the family bond means…
pages.answers:
ANSWERS — 6.3 CHILDREN’S OBLIGATIONS TO OTHER FAMILY MEMBERS
========================================

1. B. A maternal uncle
   An uncle is a relative. Classmates and workers are not family by that fact alone.

2. A. the sister of one's father
   Paternal means related through the father.

3. B. Respect, visit, help and care
   Children respect relatives, visit them, attend ceremonies, and help and care for them.

4. A. it is done to please Allah
   Intention turns a family duty into worship.

5. B. keeping the ties of kinship
   The phrase names the Islamic duty of maintaining family ties.

6. Any one: it pleases Allah; relatives help one another; children learn from elders; the family stays close; it spreads peace.
   The bond serves both worship and family life.

7. B. provision being increased and life being extended
   This is the well-known Hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari.

8. B. sending salaam, making dua and visiting when the family can
   Distance changes the method, not the duty.

9. B. greets the elders and offers help
   Greeting and helping are practical signs of respect.

10. Valuing relatives and keeping the tie through respect, visits, help and good speech.
   Appreciation is shown by maintaining the relationship.

LESSON 3: PRACTISING GOOD RELATIONSHIP WITH THE FAMILY
======================================================

## What you will learn
• Demonstrate obligations to other family members in short scenes.
• Choose ways to maintain the family bond.

Curriculum outcomes: a) outline obligations of children to other family members as an act of ibadah; c) appreciate maintaining bond with other family members

## Introduction
A visit can strengthen a family or embarrass it. The difference is in the greeting, the help you offer, and the way you speak.

## Notes
### How to behave with relatives
- Greet the oldest person first, with Assalamu alaikum, and shake hands or respond in the way your family teaches.
- Sit where you are asked to sit. Do not push cousins aside for the best place.
- Offer help before you are begged: pass plates, fetch water, or keep younger children from the cooking area if an adult asks.
- Listen when an elder is speaking. Do not correct an elder rudely, and do not whisper and laugh about them.
- At a ceremony, follow the programme. Do not wander off, demand money, or use a phone to record people without permission.
- If a grandparent is ill, a short quiet visit, a dua and a small service are better than a noisy crowd.
- Thank the hosts before you leave.

### Building the habit
Choose one relative to remember this month. It may be a grandparent or an aunt. Ask your parent the best way to show care: a visit, a drawn card with salaam, or help on a family day. Do that one thing. Then keep it up.

Good relationship is not only receiving gifts on Eid. It is also being present, useful and polite. When children do this, adults are encouraged to keep the same bond, and the family stays joined. That is the appreciation this sub-strand asks for: valuing the relatives Allah has given you and maintaining the tie.

## Key words
• aqiqah — the celebration and sacrifice for a newborn, held in the way the family observes
• host — the person whose home or event you are visiting
• elder — an older relative who should be greeted and listened to with respect

## Worked examples

### Example 1
At an uncle's house, two cousins start a loud argument over a chair while adults are talking. What should a dutiful child do?

Working:
1. The noise disrespects the elders and the host.
2. A dutiful child stops the fight, offers to share or take another seat, and apologises if needed.

Answer: Quiet the argument, give way on the chair, and show respect to the adults in the room.

## Activity: Drama: a family visit
You will need: A few chairs set out as a relative's sitting room
1. In groups, prepare a short play of a visit to a grandparent or an uncle.
2. Include a greeting, an offer of help, polite listening, and a goodbye.
3. Present the play. The class points out the obligations that were shown.
4. Each learner writes one action he or she will take this month to maintain a family bond.

## Practice
1. Whom should you greet first when you enter a room of relatives?
2. Give three good manners during a family visit or ceremony.
3. Why is a family bond not only about receiving gifts?

## Summary
• Greet elders, help hosts, and listen during visits and ceremonies.
• One real act of care is better than many unused promises.
• Maintaining the bond is how a child appreciates the family Allah has given.

### Answers to practice
1. The oldest person, or the elders, with Assalamu alaikum.
2. Any three: greet elders, sit where you are asked, offer help, listen, do not record people without permission, thank the host.
3. It is also about being present, useful and polite, and about keeping the tie to please Allah.

questions.question: Which of these is an extended family member?
questions.explanation: An uncle is a relative. Classmates and workers are not family by that fact alone.

questions.question: A paternal aunt is…
questions.explanation: Paternal means related through the father.

questions.question: Which set matches the obligations in this sub-strand?
questions.explanation: Children respect relatives, visit them, attend ceremonies, and help and care for them.

questions.question: When can helping at a family aqiqah be ibadah?
options: it is done to please Allah
it is done to show off
it is done while insulting cousins
questions.explanation: Intention turns a family duty into worship.

questions.question: Silat al-rahim means…
questions.explanation: The phrase names the Islamic duty of maintaining family ties.

questions.question: Give one benefit of fulfilling obligations to other family members.
questions.answer: Any one: it pleases Allah; relatives help one another; children learn from elders; the family stays close; it spreads peace.
questions.explanation: The bond serves both worship and family life.

questions.question: The Prophet (S.A.W) linked upholding kinship ties to which of these?
options: provision being increased and life being extended
questions.explanation: This is the well-known Hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari.

questions.question: A grandmother lives far away. How does a child maintain the bond?
options: sending salaam, making dua and visiting when the family can
questions.explanation: Distance changes the method, not the duty.

questions.question: At a relative's house the dutiful child…
options: pushes to get the best chair
greets the elders and offers help
questions.explanation: Greeting and helping are practical signs of respect.

questions.question: Appreciating the family bond means…
questions.answer: Valuing relatives and keeping the tie through respect, visits, help and good speech.
questions.explanation: Appreciation is shown by maintaining the relationship.
